newsitem.title: UK: United Utilities reassures over provisions.
newsitem.headline: United Utilities reassures over provisions.

text.p: Britain's United Utilities Plc said on Friday that it would make a provision of 83 million pounds ($135.2 million) because of problems over a Thai contract but pledged its dividend policy would not be hit.

"Following significant changes in circumstances (United) has concluded that it should make an additional prudent provision of 83 million pounds, bringing the total to 90 million pounds," the company said in a statement.
It said the move would not affect stated dividend policy and scope to return value to shareholders.
United won the contract to build a Bangkok sewerage works and system in late 1993 when it was worth 150 million pounds and should have run for 38 months.
But since then, changes in both local and national government have brought alterations in construction regulations and contract requirements, United said.
It said significant quantities of additional work were ordered and that regulations had restricted the company's ability to progress the works in critical street locations.
United said that it was "firmly of the view that...entitlement to recovery of additional costs incurred is strong, and intends to pursue recovery vigorously."
It added that provisions assumed costs were not recovered.
"It's a hefty provision but should be readily absorbed," said Yamaichi analyst Nigel Hawkins.
Another analyst said the Bangkok deal was a short-term design and operate contract and the the impact on value would be perhaps 15 pence per share.
United shares slipped to a low of 659-3/4 pence before recovering slightly to be down 61/2 pence at 667 pence by 1330GMT.

The shares were helped by United later saying it had sold its 50 percent stake in Britain's Keadby power station to its partner Scottish Hydro for 122.7 million pounds, slightly ahead of expectations.
United, which has other international interests in the Philippines, Australia, Mexico and Canada among others, said developments in Bangkok did not affect its prospects.

"The Bangkok contract is (United's) only involvement in construction activity; it has no other contracts, either in the UK or in its international activities, where it has assumed or is responsible for construction risk," United said.
As United does not have this responsibility for construction risk in its other international contracts, the prospects of further provisions should be lower, analysts said.
"We are going to remain somewhat sceptical on the profits they can wring out of international until we see more details," said David Campbell of Greig Middleton.
United was part of a consortium which won a contract to provide water and sewerage services in eastern Manila last month.
Together with Bechtel Corp of the U.S. and local conglomerate Ayala Corp, it formed the Manila Water Company (MWC).
MWC won the contract with the lowest tariff of 2.32 pesos (8 cents) a litre, well below the existing average tariff of 8.78 pesos and below other bids.

That led some analysts to query the economics of the MWC bid, especially compared with estimates from Anglian Water, part of a rival losing bid, that its higher tariff would have brought in just two to three million pounds annually.

"I am sure it is a good thing over the long term to be looking overseas, but Bangkok and Manila suggest paybacks could be a long time coming," one analyst said. ($ = 0.614 British Pounds) ($ = 26.32 Phillippine Pesos)
